newsitem.title: USA: IMF impressed by Dutch economy, but sees problems.
newsitem.headline: IMF impressed by Dutch economy, but sees problems.

text.p: The Dutch economy will grow this year and next after an "impressive" performance, but the authorities must still address structural issues on jobs and taxes, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.

A statement issued after annual IMF consultations on the Netherlands' economy predicted 3.0 percent 1997 growth, after a stronger-than-expected 2.7 percent in 1996. But above-potential output and lower unemployment and meant wages and consumer prices would both accelerate, the IMF said.
The IMF predicted 2.7 percent Dutch consumer price inflation in 1997, after 2.1 percent in 1996, but gave no figures for 1998. It said unemployment would fall to 7.0 percent from 7.8 percent in 1996.
"Growth in 1997 and 1998 is expected to remain vigorous," the IMF said. "Exports are projected to accelerate ... at the same pace as in 1996, thus supporting public consumption.
"With output likely to be at or slightly above potential and a further decline in unemployment, both wages and consumer prices are expected to accelerate somewhat."
The IMF, praising the Netherlands' private sector job creation and subdued inflation rates, said the country could become a model for others.
"The experience in the Netherlands held useful lessons for other countries, particularly with regard to the benefits of comprehensive and consistent policies sustained over a long period," it said.

It added: "It would be important to address continuing structural problems -- underlying labor force participation was low, employment among the low-skilled was still weak, there was much hidden unemployment, and the tax burden and public debt ratio, while declining, remained high."
The IMF said the Netherlands's long-standing decision to link the guilder to the mark had helped create conditions for growth. But challenges remained.

"On the eve of Economic and Monetary Union, directors underscored the need for fiscal and structural reforms to increase the flexibility of the economy, particularly in labor and product markets," it said.
